A stranger convinced a McDonald's manager to strip-search her own employee, take her clothes, and hand her over to people who would abuse her.
And he controlled the entire situation from miles away.
With one phone call.
It's April ninth, two thousand four, in Kentucky.
An assistant manager answers the restaurant phone.
A man introduces himself as Officer Scott.
He claims an employee has stolen a customer's purse.
The manager recognizes the girl immediately.
eighteen-year-old Louise Ogborn.
He asks the manager to bring her into the office.
Then the instructions begin.
Search her.
Make her remove her clothes.
Find someone to watch her.
Each order goes a little further, but the caller presents it as part of an official police investigation.
One employee is so disturbed by what's happening that she walks out.
But the manager doesn't stop.
She brings in her own fiancé, Walter Nix, to watch Louise.
And the situation turns into a sexual assault.
For more than three hours, the stranger on the phone continues giving orders.
Then a fifty-eight-year-old maintenance worker named Tom Simms takes the phone.
He listens.
He questions what's happening.
And when the caller gives him instructions, Tom refuses.
He says NO.
And suddenly, the authority the caller had over everyone starts to collapse.
The manager contacts her supervisor.
The answer?
Nobody from the police had called.
There was no Officer Scott.
No investigation.
No stolen purse.
The entire situation had been controlled by a stranger pretending to be a police officer.
And this wasn't an isolated incident.
Similar calls had targeted businesses across thirty-two states.
Investigators eventually arrested a Florida security guard named David Stewart.
But a jury acquitted him.
Now, think about what actually happened here.
The caller didn't walk into that restaurant with a weapon.
He didn't physically force anyone to follow his orders.
He created a situation where every small act of obedience made the next, more disturbing demand easier to accept.
And that's what makes this case so terrifying.
Sometimes, the most dangerous part of an order isn't what it asks you to do.
It's the fact that you've already said yes...
to the one before it.
